MUJAHID:v2p762#3/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p762#3/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p762#3/r1.claim: Mujahid says the day illuminates the sun.

FARRA:v3p266/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r2.claim: The kasra in rhyming forms from wāw roots follows the yāʾ-based pattern begun in the sūra; a sequence beginning in wāw could instead take fatḥa throughout.

FARRA:v3p266/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r3.claim: Ḥamza's opening of wāw-derived forms while keeping kasra on yāʾ forms shows poor grasp of Arabic patterns; with wāw alone he prefers fatḥa, while yāʾ permits either vowel.

FARRA:v3p266/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p266/r5.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p266/r5.claim: The day reveals the darkness; its feminine object is omitted because it is understood, as in Arabic phrases about a cold morning or evening.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p529#4/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p529#4/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p529#4/r1.claim: The day reveals the darkness or the world.

TUSTARI:91:3/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:91:3/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:91:3/r1.claim: The day is the light of faith: it dispels ignorance’s darkness and extinguishes the flame of Hell.

TAB-FULL:v24p437/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p437/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p437/r1.claim: The verse says daytime makes the sun apparent; although the alternative grammatical reading has a rationale, he prefers the explanation reported by the early authorities.

TAB-FULL:v24p437/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p437/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p437/r2.claim: Qatadah says daytime covers the sun.

TAB-FULL:v24p437/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p437/r3.speaker: بعض أهل العربية
TAB-FULL:v24p437/r3.claim: Some grammarians take the pronoun to refer to darkness: daytime reveals the darkness, with a feminine pronoun for an understood, previously unmentioned referent.

ZAJJAJ:v5p331#2/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p331#2/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p331#2/r2.claim: The day reveals the darkness, which is understood though unstated, like saying “our morning became cold”; alternatively, daylight reveals the sun as it spreads.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r12.claim: Qatadah identifies the sun with daytime, the moon as following the new moon at its setting, and daylight as covering the sun.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r3.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3437/r3.claim: Mujahid says the day makes the sun clear and bright.

NAHHAS:v5p235/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p235/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p235/r3.claim: The day makes the sun visible, which is the clear sense; al-Farrāʾ's darkness reading is remote because darkness was not mentioned.

THALABI:v10p212#3/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p212#3/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p212#3/r5.claim: One reading takes the daylight as making the sun clear and revealing it through its brightness.

THALABI:v10p212#3/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p212#3/r6.speaker: الفراء وجماعة من العلماء
THALABI:v10p212#3/r6.claim: They say daylight reveals the darkness; a feminine pronoun may refer to a familiar omitted feminine noun whose meaning is understood.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r13.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r13.claim: Mujahid says daylight illuminates the sun and removes the night's darkness.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r14.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r14.claim: Mawardi also reads the phrase as the day making the sun manifest, citing Qays ibn al-Khatim's verse as evidence for ظهور.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r15.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p281#2/r15.claim: He further allows that daytime reveals the earth's creatures after their concealment at night.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r1.claim: Tajli means making visible and uncovering, as also explained in the discussion of the Hour not being disclosed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r2.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r2.claim: The day makes the sun clear by removing darkness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r3.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p52/r3.claim: The feminine pronoun can refer to understood darkness even when darkness is not explicitly named, as in ordinary statements that morning or evening is cold.

WAHIDI-QT:91:3/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:91:3/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:91:3/r1.claim: The day reveals and removes the darkness.

WAHIDI-QT:91:3/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:91:3/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:91:3/r2.claim: Another view says daylight reveals the sun, which becomes visible as the day spreads.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:91:1-8/r3.claim: Day uncovers darkness; another view says it reveals and shows the sun as the day spreads.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p435#2/r3.claim: Day reveals darkness, with the unspoken object understood because it is obvious.

KASHSHAF:91:3/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:91:3/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:91:3/r1.claim: The day reveals the sun as it expands, when the sun becomes fully visible.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r3.claim: The day ‘reveals’ the sun when it swells and spreads and the sun becomes fully clear; the pronoun may instead refer to darkness, the world, or the earth, understood from context.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p762/r5.claim: The repeated wāws can govern both accusative and genitive: the oath-wāw omits its verb altogether and substitutes for it, while coordinated wāws inherit that double function, resolving the apparent two-governor problem.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r11.claim: The immediate context suggests daytime begins at sunrise; al-Zajjaj and others say it begins at dawn, and both end at sunset.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r12.speaker: الزجاج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r12.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the day begins at dawn.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r13.speaker: الزجاج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p487#2/r13.claim: The pronoun in جلاها may refer to the sun, earth, or unmentioned darkness supplied by context; jalla means uncover and illuminate.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:91:1-15/r8.claim: The day unveils darkness; the feminine pronoun can refer to darkness even though the noun is omitted because the meaning is clear.

TABRISI:91:1-15/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:91:1-15/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:91:1-15/r9.claim: Alternatively, the day unveils the sun by making its visible body appear.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138/r1.claim: The pronoun means the sun: daylight makes it clear as daylight spreads.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138/r2.speaker: الفراء واللغويون
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p138/r2.claim: Alternatively, it refers to an unmentioned darkness, understood from context, as in saying that the morning was cold and a north wind blew.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r1.claim: The sura urges obedience and warns against disobedience; oaths by beneficial created things prompt reflection and gratitude because divine oaths weigh heavily on the heart.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r5.claim: Al-Farra explains imala in endings with roots from waw by their resemblance to words beginning with ya; forms such as tala and daha can shift toward ya in verbs.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r6.claim: Full non-imala is also sound because many Arabs do not incline these alifs toward ya, and letters that historically shifted from waw or ya do not always reveal the shift in pronunciation.

RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p171/r7.claim: Hamza's mixed approach is also good: only alifs derived from ya warrant imala, while tala, daha and similar forms derive from waw.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.speaker: القفال
RAZI-FULL:v31p173#2/r2.claim: Al-Qaffal says all four oaths are really about the sun through its midday light, the moon's borrowing its light, its emergence in daytime and its concealment at night.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173/r1.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v31p173/r1.claim: Al-Zajjaj makes the pronoun in 'reveals it' refer to the sun: daylight is the sun's light, and the strength of the effect indicates the strength of its cause.

RAZI-FULL:v31p173/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p173/r2.speaker: الجمهور
RAZI-FULL:v31p173/r2.claim: Most commentators take the pronoun to refer to darkness, the world or the earth, despite no explicit prior mention, as in ordinary Arabic usage.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r1.speaker: الفراء والكلبي
QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r1.claim: The day reveals darkness even though darkness is not explicitly mentioned, as in saying 'the morning became cool' for 'our morning became cool.'

QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r2.speaker: بعض المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r2.claim: Others take the pronoun as referring to the sun: daylight reveals the sun's body by its light, as Qays ibn al-Khatim's poem illustrates.

QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r3.speaker: بعض المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:91:3/r3.claim: Alternatively, daytime reveals earth's animals as they emerge from nighttime hiding, or it reveals the world or earth, though not previously named.

BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:91:1-4/r3.claim: Daylight reveals the sun, darkness, the world, or earth, even where the latter is not named.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r1.claim: The day reveals the sun to observers as daylight spreads, when it becomes fully clear.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r2.speaker: قيل
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r2.claim: One reported interpretation makes the pronoun refer to darkness.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r3.speaker: قيل
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r3.claim: Another reported interpretation makes the pronoun refer to the world, although it was not previously mentioned.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r4.speaker: قيل
NASAFI-FULL:v4p341#6/r4.claim: Another reported interpretation makes the pronoun refer to the earth, although it was not previously mentioned; the author compares this to a verse that mentions creatures on its surface.

QASHANI:91:1-3/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:91:1-3/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:91:1-3/r3.claim: Day is the spirit’s dominance and full light, displaying the soul as midday displays the sun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p484/r7.claim: The Meccan surah swears by parts of the upper and lower worlds and by the soul as an instrument of reflection; it moves from disbelievers' afterlife to their worldly destruction and eventual Fire.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r13.claim: The apparent object of jallāhā is the sun, fully revealed as daylight spreads.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r14.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r14.claim: Other explanations make the pronoun refer to darkness, the earth, or the world; the agent that clears darkness is the sun or day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r15.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p485/r15.claim: A further possibility makes God the subject: the day is when God reveals the sun, its fullest state.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r3.claim: For eloquence, all the pronouns through يغشاها should refer to the sun; this matches the preceding description of day revealing it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.speaker: القفال
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p486/r5.claim: Al-Qaffāl summarizes the oaths as four solar aspects: daytime brightness and activity, the moon taking its light, full appearance, and disappearance at night.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.speaker: أصحابنا
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r1.claim: The author's colleagues interpret سبحان من سخركن as a proper name, with mā infinitival and temporal.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r1.claim: The Shaykh invokes the Sibawayh poem as a case of coordinating a genitive plus nominative pair with another pair; the author says this concedes the disputed coordination, though the poem has an additional complication.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.speaker: الخليل
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r2.claim: Al-Khalil says the last two wāws in the oath sequence coordinate nouns, while the first is like the prepositional wāw and the tā’ of swearing.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.speaker: ابن كيسان
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r3.claim: Ibn Kaysan permits an explicit oath verb with the wāw, as in ‘I swear by God that Zayd is standing’; the author says this objection does not bind al-Zamakhshari’s position.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#2/r4.claim: The Shaykh identifies the deeper puzzle as finding a governor for a future ‘idha’ after an oath: the present oath verb, an implied event, the oath object itself, and an implied circumstantial all face objections.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r1.claim: The Shaykh’s preference that conjunction does not itself govern does not compel al-Zamakhshari, who chooses the alternative grammatical doctrine.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r2.claim: The author insists that the construction does involve two governors: oath wāw governs the genitive and the oath verb governs the time adverb, with both sets of complements coordinated.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r3.claim: The Sibawayh poem cited by the Shaykh acknowledges coordination across the two governors, even though the Shaykh relies on Sibawayh’s authority.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r4.claim: Mentioning Ibn Kaysan’s permission to state an oath verb does not refute al-Zamakhshari, because the latter need not share Ibn Kaysan’s view.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r5.claim: The Shaykh’s example with a second time phrase preceding the coordinated noun does parallel the verse’s governors, though it raises a separate issue of repeating the construction.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r6.claim: Al-Khalil’s description as ‘disfavored’ supports prohibition rather than rebutting al-Zamakhshari; the Shaykh has either softened the term or misunderstood it.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r7.claim: An omitted construct such as ‘rising of the star’ can be the governor; the author says an oath now may refer to an object that will exist later, so the tense mismatch is no objection.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r8.claim: A deleted governor before ‘idha’ is possible as a prospective circumstantial; the oath verb still governs it, and the circumstantial may be understood prospectively.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3#3/r9.claim: If the sworn object is a physical entity, one can supply an event, making the temporal phrase a circumstantial attached to that event; Ibn al-Hajib addressed the question and the author notes extended debate.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r1.claim: For ‘jallaha’, the subject may be the pronoun of daylight or may refer to God; its object pronoun may refer to the sun, darkness, the world, or the earth.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r2.claim: The ‘idha’ clauses raise a syntactic problem: a conditional needs an answer, while a purely temporal phrase needs a governor; the oath verb is present-time and cannot straightforwardly govern a future time phrase.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari answers that an oath wāw suppresses its verb and stands for both the verb and preposition; following coordinating wāws can therefore govern the same accusative and genitive pattern.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r4.claim: The Shaykh rejects the claim that a conjunction governs by standing in for a governor; he says the governor of the coordinated element is the same as for its antecedent, though he does not insist on that point against al-Zamakhshari.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r5.claim: The Shaykh says the verse coordinates two nouns with matching case roles, rather than coordinating across two governors, and offers ‘passing by Zayd standing and ‘Amr sitting’ as the pattern.

SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:91:2-3/r6.claim: The Shaykh cites a line in Sibawayh that coordinates a genitive and a nominative with another genitive and nominative as a parallel construction.

IBNKATHIR:91:3/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r2.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r2.claim: The day covers the sun with its light.

IBNKATHIR:91:3/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r3.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r3.claim: Some Arabists take the object to be unmentioned darkness, so the phrase means when day clears the darkness.

IBNKATHIR:91:3/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r4.claim: The pronoun refers to the earth's surface, which day makes plain; this also fits the following oath about night covering it and Mujāhid's parallel at al-Layl 92:2.

IBNKATHIR:91:3/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r5.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r5.claim: After saying the plain reading is more apt, the author cites Mujahid’s related phrasing at al-Layl 92:2.

IBNKATHIR:91:3/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r6.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR:91:3/r6.claim: Ibn Jarīr instead makes the pronoun refer to the sun throughout, because it was already mentioned.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p437#2/r6.claim: Day is the time for activity and displays the sun in changing conditions; likewise the body may purify or soil the soul and intellect, producing an angelic person when aligned with reason or a devilish one when opposed.

DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p527/r8.claim: He glossed the sun as its light, the moon as following it, daylight as illuminating it, God as builder of heaven, the earth as spread out, inspiration as showing good and evil, and corruption as leading astray.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r1.claim: Although the conditional sense of idha seems to require an answer and an operator, the author reads it causally in these oaths: swear because the moon follows, the day reveals, and the night covers; al-Qamus also allows a present-time meaning, “when.”

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r2.claim: Day is the sun's light erasing the earth's shadow and night-darkness; it reveals the sun as daylight spreads, so the act of revealing is figuratively attributed to the day because it occurs then.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r3.claim: The text may also mean that day reveals the darkness, world, or earth, though these objects are omitted because they are understood.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r4.claim: In the inward reading, day is the spirit's dominant light and power, bringing the spirit fully into view like the sun at midday.

BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p341#2/r7.claim: The oath wa's are conjunctive and share the implied verb, avoiding the problem of coordinating words governed by different agents or multiplying oaths with one answer.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r1.claim: The day displays the sun as daylight spreads and time passes; the attribution is figurative. This reading best preserves the explicit referent and consistent pronouns.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r2.claim: Other readings take the pronoun to refer to Earth, the world (meaning its surface), or darkness, which the day removes.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p141/r3.claim: A reading with God as the implicit subject, making the verse swear by day when God displays the sun in its fullest state, is far-fetched.

ELMALILI:91:3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:3/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:3/r1.claim: Tajliyah means to make manifest, clarify, or polish; the pronoun refers to the sun, and the phrase describes clear daylight without cloud or haze.

ELMALILI:91:3/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:3/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:3/r2.claim: Daylight is made the agent that unveils the sun even though it is the sun's own light reflected on earth, a noteworthy rhetorical reversal.

ELMALILI:91:3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:3/r3.claim: An unobstructed day makes light clearer, and clear light makes the sun more manifest; through light the sun is sensed, while clouds leave it known indirectly by reason.

ELMALILI:91:3/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:91:3/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:91:3/r4.claim: The oath draws attention to manifestation in the horizons and within the self, and to how an effect points to its effective cause.

QUTB-ZILAL:91:3/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:91:3/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:91:3/r1.claim: The daytime’s disclosure suggests that al-duha means the specific morning period, not all day; the pronoun apparently returns to the sun but also subtly evokes the earth it reveals.

QUTB-ZILAL:91:3/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:91:3/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:91:3/r2.claim: Daylight uncovers the world and affects human life; because people grow used to it and forget its beauty, the brief oath awakens reflection on this great phenomenon.

IBNASHUR:91:3/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:3/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:3/r1.claim: The feminine pronoun in jallaha most naturally refers to the sun: the day makes the sun appear, with manifestation figuratively attributed to the day; the oath is by day as evidence of the earth's precise order.

IBNASHUR:91:3/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:3/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:3/r2.claim: Another view takes the pronoun to refer to earth: daylight illuminates and unveils the earth to observers, as people say rain was sent when they mean the sky sent its water.

IBNASHUR:91:3/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:3/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:3/r3.claim: Restricting the oath to the time of manifestation incorporates a reminder of divine favor.

IBNASHUR:91:3/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:3/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:3/r4.claim: The sun and its direct and reflected lights symbolize faith emerging after disbelief and piety after sin, since darkness represents sin and light represents faith and obedience.

IBNASHUR:91:3/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:91:3/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:91:3/r5.claim: Night follows day in the oath because it is the opposing period of darkness.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r1.claim: The oath confirms the threat of destruction implicitly conveyed by the news; each waw following a pause is an oath particle, and the sun, moon, sky, earth, and human soul display God's wise and powerful creation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p366/r2.claim: The dawn brightness, moon following the sun, daylight, and night are all examples of the fine order God established.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p368/r2.claim: إذا is a circumstantial time adverb attached to the state of each moon, day, and night; each is sworn by in the condition that best displays God's artistry.

TABATABAI:91:1-8/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r4.claim: The feminine pronoun refers to earth: daytime reveals it to sight. The alternative takes day as agent and the sun as object, but this reverses the fact that the sun causes daylight.

TABATABAI:91:1-8/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:91:1-8/r5.claim: Other proposals refer the pronoun to the world or darkness, or make God the agent and sun the object; the author calls these distant readings.

ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n2/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n2/r1.speaker: Zamakhshari
ASAD-NOTES:91:1#n2/r1.claim: Zamakhshari takes the pronoun 'it' to indicate the world or the earth.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r1.claim: Qur'anic oaths probably draw on a characteristic expression of pre-Islamic soothsayers, though the connection remains insufficiently researched.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:anmerkung/r2.claim: The structure and function of cumulative oath series are discussed at 93:1–2, with many parallels.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r1.claim: An eight-verse oath series leads into the antithetical statement in verses 9–10; the pre-Islamic genre is repurposed in verses 5–7 to express biblical creation ideas.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r2.claim: The series moves through three complementary or contrasting pairs—sun/moon, night/day, heaven/earth—then the soul, whose opposed moral capacities are specified in verse 8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r4.claim: The oath series narrows from cosmic creation, traced vertically from celestial bodies to earth, to the human moral subject.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r5.claim: Its shift from creation to humanity resembles the 81:1–14 sequence, which evokes the world's eschatological dissolution rather than cyclical operation.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1-8:kommentar/r6.claim: A caesura after verse 4 divides effects and activities of the oath's objects in verses 1–4 from references to God's creating activity in verses 5–8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:1:anmerkung/r2.claim: The translation signals paired oaths by beginning verses 2, 4, and 6 with and, following Neuwirth.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:2:anmerkung/r2.claim: One might translate talā as the moon falling behind the sun, but the parallel between verses 1–3 and 2–4 favors the moon's following the day into night.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r1.claim: The wording is closely related to 92:1–2, pairing night with yaġšā and day with tajallā or jallā.

CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:91:3-4:anmerkung/r2.claim: Verse 3 effectively paraphrases the ḍuḥā already named in verse 1.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p329/r2.claim: The world appears to contain opposing forces, yet God keeps them within limits and in harmony; their accord preserves the universe.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r1.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night are complementary phenomena; their apparent oppositions in appearance, temperament, and effects serve in harmony.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p331/r2.claim: Earlier sūrahs used this complementarity for arguments about monotheism and the Day of Judgement; here the focus is how the apparent opposites work together.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r1.claim: The cosmic order prevents the sun or moon from intruding on the other’s appointed time and keeps day and night within their roles, as 36:40 says.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p332/r2.claim: Harmony among opposites sustains the universe; their obedience to limits teaches people to stay within God’s bounds, since exceeding them creates disorder God will not tolerate.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r6.claim: Some take 91:9–10 as the oath’s complement; Islahi gives weight to al-Zamakhsharī’s rejection of that view.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p335/r7.claim: The sun, moon, day, and night show that a powerful, self-sustaining God keeps the world’s elements on their appointed paths, preventing their collision from destroying it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p336/r3.claim: Suppressing the complement lets everything evident from the oaths count as its content; one prominent implication is that God destroys rebellious nations.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:91:1/r1.claim: Oaths by natural phenomena highlight cosmic order and its benefits, the Creator's power, and the importance of what follows.

STUDYQURAN:91:3/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:3/r1.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:91:3/r1.claim: The day disclosing it may refer to the sun.

STUDYQURAN:91:3/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:3/r2.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:91:3/r2.claim: The referent may instead be the world or earth.

STUDYQURAN:91:3/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:3/r3.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:91:3/r3.claim: It may refer to darkness, making the sense “by the day when dispersing it.”

STUDYQURAN:91:3/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:91:3/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:91:3/r4.claim: Spiritually, the verse evokes faith's light extinguishing the darkness of ignorance.
